name: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism

clinicalPearls: Glycogen storage diseases (GSDs) are inherited defects of glycogen metabolism producing glycogen that is abnormal in structure and/or quantity; collectively their prevalence is estimated at roughly 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 25,000 live births, with most being autosomal recessive and a minority X-linked or autosomal dominant.

GSDs are grouped by the predominant organ affected (liver vs muscle). The most common childhood forms are glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (GSD I), acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency (GSD II/Pompe), debrancher deficiency (GSD III), and liver phosphorylase kinase deficiency (GSD IX); the most common adult form is myophosphorylase deficiency (GSD V/McArdle).

GSD I (von Gierke) classically presents around 3-4 months with hepatomegaly, doll-like facies with round cheeks, thin extremities, short stature, and a protuberant abdomen; lab hallmarks are fasting hypoketotic hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and elevated LDL with low HDL producing milky/cloudy serum.

A key distinction of GSD III from GSD I is that lactate and uric acid are normal in GSD III, whereas aminotransferases and urine glucose tetrasaccharide (Glc4) are markedly elevated early then decline with age; GSD III hypoglycemia is typically ketotic and gluconeogenesis remains intact (unlike GSD I, which impairs both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis).

GSD I type Ib differs from Ia by additional neutropenia and impaired neutrophil function, causing recurrent bacterial infections, mucosal ulceration, inflammatory-bowel-disease-like findings, and periodontal disease.

Pompe disease (GSD II) is unique in storing glycogen primarily within lysosomes rather than cytoplasm; classic infantile-onset disease presents with hypotonia, generalized weakness, macroglossia, and rapidly progressive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with death usually before age 2 if untreated, whereas late-onset disease is defined by absence of cardiomyopathy in the first year and slowly progressive proximal/respiratory (diaphragm) weakness.

McArdle disease (GSD V) is a prototypical muscle-energy disorder with exercise-induced cramps, myalgia, weakness, and myoglobinuria; the characteristic 'second wind' phenomenon (continuing exercise pain-free after a brief rest, as fatty-acid oxidation takes over) is unique to GSD V and there is no rise in blood lactate with exercise.

Tarui disease (GSD VII, phosphofructokinase-M deficiency) mimics GSD V but shows an 'out of wind' phenomenon worsened by carbohydrate-rich meals and exercise, no spontaneous second wind, plus compensated hemolysis and hyperuricemia; giving IV dextrose or pre-exercise simple carbohydrates is detrimental in GSD VII (opposite to GSD V).

In a young male with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) pattern on ECG strongly suggests Danon disease (X-linked LAMP2), where the WPW prevalence is about five times that in idiopathic/familial HCM.

Classic galactosemia (GALT deficiency) presents after milk feeding with vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, hepatomegaly, aminoaciduria, and a notable susceptibility to gram-negative (especially E. coli) sepsis that may precede diagnosis; even with early dietary galactose elimination, long-term outcomes remain poor (speech/learning disorders, cataracts, primary ovarian insufficiency in females).

Hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency) patients are asymptomatic until fructose/sucrose/sorbitol is ingested, then develop postprandial hypoglycemia, jaundice, hepatomegaly, vomiting, and convulsions; affected children characteristically develop an aversion to sweets.
Genetic/molecular testing has largely replaced invasive tissue biopsy for diagnosis and subtyping of many GSDs; Pompe disease is now on the U.S. recommended uniform newborn screening panel.
harrison.pathophysiology: Glycogen is the branched storage polymer of glucose, formed from alpha-1,4 chains branched by alpha-1,6 linkages. Inherited enzyme defects along glycogen synthesis, glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, and the linked galactose/fructose pathways disrupt glucose homeostasis. In GSD I, deficient glucose-6-phosphatase (Ia) or its translocase (Ib) blocks the final conversion of glucose-6-phosphate to glucose, impairing both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and causing fasting hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis and secondary hyperuricemia and hyperlipidemia. In disorders of glycogenolysis with intact gluconeogenesis (GSD III debrancher, GSD VI liver phosphorylase, GSD IX phosphorylase kinase), incomplete glycogen breakdown causes hepatomegaly and milder, often ketotic hypoglycemia. GSD IV (brancher deficiency) produces poorly soluble abnormal glycogen (polyglucosan) injuring liver, heart, muscle, and nervous system. Pompe disease (GSD II) results from lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency causing lysosomal glycogen accumulation in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Muscle-energy GSDs (V/McArdle myophosphorylase, VII/Tarui phosphofructokinase, and rarer defects of phosphoglycerate mutase, LDH-A, aldolase A, beta-enolase) limit ATP generation from glycogenolysis/glycolysis, producing exercise intolerance, cramps, and rhabdomyolysis. In galactosemia, deficiency along the Leloir pathway (most commonly GALT) leads to accumulation of toxic galactose-1-phosphate injuring liver, kidney, brain, lens, and ovary. In hereditary fructose intolerance, aldolase B deficiency causes fructose-1-phosphate accumulation and ATP depletion that inhibits gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of infantile/childhood hepatomegaly with hypoglycemia (fatty acid oxidation defects, gluconeogenesis defects such as fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency)
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy of other etiology (idiopathic/familial HCM) versus glycogenoses with cardiac involvement (Pompe, Danon, PRKAG2)
Polymyositis/inflammatory myopathy (McArdle disease may mimic on EMG)
Other metabolic myopathies and channelopathies presenting with exercise intolerance and rhabdomyolysis
Neonatal sepsis and other inborn errors presenting with jaundice and hepatomegaly (versus galactosemia and hereditary fructose intolerance)
infectionMimics: Gram-negative (E. coli) neonatal sepsis can be the presenting feature of classic galactosemia and may precede the metabolic diagnosis
Recurrent bacterial infections, oral/intestinal mucosal ulceration, and periodontal disease in GSD Ib due to neutropenia and neutrophil dysfunction
nonInfectiousMimics: Idiopathic or familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (mimicked by Pompe, Danon, PRKAG2 syndrome)
Polymyositis (McArdle disease may produce inflammatory-appearing EMG)
Statin-induced myopathy/rhabdomyolysis (patients with GSD V and VII are at increased risk and may be confused with primary statin myopathy)
Polycystic ovarian syndrome features (hirsutism, irregular menses) reported in GSD I and GSD III
additionalInvestigations: Fasting glucose, lactate, and uric acid (lactate/uric acid normal in GSD III but elevated in GSD I)
Lipid profile (hypertriglyceridemia, elevated LDL, low HDL in GSD I)
Serum aminotransferases and urine glucose tetrasaccharide (Glc4) as biomarkers in GSD II, III, and IX
Serum creatine kinase (may be normal despite muscle involvement; not always elevated in late-onset Pompe)
Blood ketones during fasting/illness for liver GSDs
Molecular/genetic testing (e.g., AGL, GBE1, PYGL, PHKA2/PHKB/PHKG2, GAA, PYGM, PFKM, GALT, aldolase B genes) now preferred over biopsy
Enzyme assays (e.g., acid alpha-glucosidase in blood/fibroblasts/muscle for Pompe; CRIM status determination)
Nonischemic forearm exercise test for suspected muscle GSD (abnormal lactate response); ischemic test largely abandoned
ECG (high-voltage QRS and short PR in infantile Pompe; WPW pattern in Danon/PRKAG2), echocardiography, and cardiac/muscle MRI or ultrasound
Liver biopsy/histology and abdominal imaging (CT/MRI surveillance for hepatocellular adenoma and carcinoma in liver GSDs)
Newborn screening (Pompe on the U.S. RUSP; galactosemia screening programs)
redFlags: Neonatal/infant hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis (GSD I) or with sepsis-like presentation
Rapidly progressive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and heart failure in infancy (infantile Pompe; congenital PRKAG2; massive myocardial glycogen deposition)
WPW pattern with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in a young male (Danon disease)
Burgundy/dark urine with myoglobinuria after strenuous exercise (rhabdomyolysis) risking acute renal failure and acute compartment syndrome in muscle GSDs
Respiratory insufficiency/failure as a presenting or progressive feature of late-onset Pompe disease
Easy bruising, epistaxis, and prolonged bleeding time from platelet dysfunction/acquired von Willebrand-like disease in GSD I
Hepatocellular adenoma with hemorrhage or malignant transformation to hepatocellular carcinoma in liver GSDs (I, III, IV, VI, IX)
Risk of malignant hyperthermia with halogenated anesthetics/muscle relaxants in GSD V and VII
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis varies widely by disorder and treatment. GSD I requires lifelong fasting avoidance; survivors face long-term gout, osteopenia/osteoporosis, hepatocellular adenoma with potential HCC, progressive renal disease/proteinuria advancing to end-stage renal disease, and increased pancreatitis and cardiovascular risk. GSD III liver disease often appears to improve in childhood but can progress to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and HCC, while GSD IIIa muscle and cardiac disease may worsen after the third-fourth decade with risk of sudden death from arrhythmia. Classic infantile Pompe disease is fatal within about 2 years untreated, but enzyme replacement therapy has substantially improved survival in both infantile and late-onset forms; CRIM-negative patients fare worse without immunomodulation. McArdle disease has a generally good prognosis with lifestyle measures, and physically active patients do better than inactive ones. Andersen disease (GSD IV) classic hepatic form is often fatal before age 5 without liver transplantation. Danon disease carries a poor prognosis with progressive end-stage heart failure in early adulthood. Classic galactosemia has poor long-term neurodevelopmental and ovarian outcomes despite early diet, whereas clinical-variant galactosemia and well-treated hereditary fructose intolerance generally have good prognoses; benign fructosuria and biochemical-variant (Duarte) galactosemia are essentially benign.
pitfalls: Normal serum creatine kinase does not exclude muscle involvement, including in late-onset Pompe disease, and normal muscle histology or EMG can occur due to disease heterogeneity.
GSD VI and hepatic GSD IX were historically considered benign but show clinical heterogeneity, with reported fibrosis, cirrhosis, HCA, and HCC, including in the X-linked form.
Giving IV dextrose or pre-exercise simple carbohydrates worsens GSD VII (Tarui), the opposite of the beneficial effect of pre-exercise carbohydrate in GSD V (McArdle).
PRKAG2 syndrome can be misdiagnosed as infantile-onset Pompe disease due to phenotypic similarity of severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Diagnosing galactokinase (type II) deficiency is often missed because many newborn screening programs measure GALT activity rather than galactose directly, so it requires excluding GALT deficiency.

Complete galactose elimination is NOT recommended in GALE deficiency (type III), because galactose is needed for nervous-system structural proteins and these patients cannot synthesize UDP-galactose from glucose; dietary restriction rather than elimination is used.
The traditional discrete hepatic versus neuromuscular subtyping of GSD IV is now viewed as an oversimplification; it is better conceptualized as a multidimensional clinical continuum.
McArdle disease may mimic inflammatory myopathy/polymyositis on EMG, risking misdiagnosis.
harrison.severityClassification: Several GSDs are stratified by clinical severity and onset. Pompe disease (GSD II): classic infantile-onset (cardiomyopathy at/near birth, fatal within ~2 years untreated, GAA typically <1%), nonclassic infantile-onset (less severe cardiomyopathy, slower progression), and late-onset (no cardiomyopathy in first year, slowly progressive proximal/respiratory weakness, GAA ~2-35%); CRIM-positive versus CRIM-negative status further guides immunomodulation. GSD III is subclassified IIIa (~85%, liver plus cardiac/skeletal muscle) versus IIIb (~15%, liver only). GSD I is divided into Ia (~80%) and Ib (~20%, with neutropenia/neutrophil dysfunction). GSD IV/Andersen spans a continuum from lethal perinatal/congenital neuromuscular forms through classic progressive and nonprogressive hepatic forms to adult polyglucosan body disease (APBD). Galactosemia type I is graded as classic (absent/barely detectable GALT, severe), clinical variant (residual activity, milder, common in African Americans), and biochemical/Duarte variant (asymptomatic).
